content: The facility-based HIV patient card serves as the primary data source for other tools within the HIV patient monitoring system. It contains the complete HIV-specific minimum dataset. In some settings, this card may also be referred to as a patient record or file. It includes detailed information such as reproductive and family planning choices (including current pregnancy status), antenatal care (ANC) number, child vaccinations, tests for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and their results, nutritional support and infant-feeding practices (including current breastfeeding status), and the status of HIV-exposed infants. For HIV-exposed infants, the card records their name, date of birth, cotrimoxazole (CTX) prophylaxis, type of HIV test, test results, final status, and a unique ID once confirmed as HIV-positive. The HIV patient card is divided into three sections. The front page provides a summary of the patient’s demographic information, family details, HIV care, and antiretroviral therapy (ART) information. The second section, known as the encounter page, documents each clinical visit in a row, starting with the baseline visit. When the page is full, additional blank photocopies can be attached to the card. During each clinical visit, health workers are required to check and record the information in the columns using the code boxes provided as a guide. The third section summarizes patient education and counseling, including adherence support. This section can be completed by the same health worker who filled out the encounter form or by a counselor or educator in the clinic. It is essential to prioritize key points during each visit and document them succinctly and legibly to facilitate follow-up. The card has undergone several revisions. On the front of the card, new recommendations include starting the card at the point of entry, assigning a unique ID to all patients enrolling in HIV care (regardless of ART start date), and discontinuing its use for HIV-exposed infants prior to confirmation of HIV infection. Other changes include updates to reflect differentiated care models, simplified family status (with the addition of the date of death), inclusion of the date of the first HIV-positive test, and updates to relevant chronic conditions and concomitant medications. A new box for tuberculosis (TB) status has been added, along with third-line ART regimens and date columns for follow-up status. The encounter page has also been updated. Additions include a column for vaccinations under pregnancy/reproductive health (RH) and family planning (FP) choices, a column for hepatitis status/information, and changes to column titles such as Treatment-limiting toxicities/adverse reactions and Comorbidities and coinfections. The term isoniazid (INH) has been replaced with TB preventive therapy, and Pills dispensed has been replaced with Record start or complete. ART adherence is now recorded as the Number of missed doses, and the investigations column has been revised. The codes page of the card has been updated to include changes to codes for pregnancy/RH-FP choices, FP methods, comorbidities and coinfections, TB status, TB specimen tests and results, treatment-limiting toxicities, reasons for non-adherence, ARV drug substitution or stopping ART, and HIV-exposed infant final status. Vaccination codes and codes for hepatitis information have also been added. The back of the card, which focuses on follow-up education, now includes information on prevention interventions, infection control (for TB), hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) interventions, and date columns. Line items have been revised to simplify and prioritize interventions. Community-based patient monitoring tools have been introduced under the differentiated care model recommended by WHO. Stable HIV patients on ART may require less frequent clinical visits and medication pickups and can access decentralized service delivery points, including community-based services. To accommodate the growing number of patients in HIV care programs, WHO recommends task-shifting to allow clinical settings to focus on patients initiating treatment or those who are unwell, while stable patients are monitored by supervised lay providers. Community health workers (CHWs) may engage in activities such as HIV testing, counseling, referral, medication distribution, psychosocial support, adherence monitoring, and linking patients to community-based support groups. CHWs must routinely monitor and report on a minimum set of actions in a standardized manner. Patient monitoring plays a critical role in linking community and facility health workers. CHWs using their own tools must reconcile the information collected with the facility-based ART register, which serves as the main aggregation tool for cross-sectional or cohort reports. If CHWs distribute ARVs in the community, their records must also align with pharmacy dispensing records. The HIV transfer or referral form ensures continuity of care when patients are referred or transferred between facilities. A minimum amount of information, primarily from the front of the HIV patient card, should accompany the patient to maximize retention on ART and viral suppression while avoiding duplication in record-keeping. The form includes a counter-referral section to notify the referring facility of a successful transfer. The ART register contains key information from the HIV patient card and is organized by the month and year (cohort) in which the patient starts ART. It tracks patient follow-up over time, including CD4 count and viral load, and aggregates data into ART cohort and HIV cross-sectional reports. WHO recommends maintaining ART registers at all treatment sites, including antenatal care (ANC) and TB clinics, to facilitate data reconciliation and longitudinal follow-up of patient cohorts. The updated ART register includes 20 rows, with one row per patient. The first page records demographic information, ART start status, key co-treatments, pregnancies, and regimen changes, while subsequent pages track monthly follow-up for up to 10 years. Follow-up status (e.g., on ART, stopped, lost to follow-up, transferred out, or deceased) is recorded in the top row, while pregnancy or breastfeeding status is recorded in the bottom row. CD4 and viral load test dates and results are documented at key intervals. Consistent with the treat all approach, patients diagnosed with HIV should be enrolled in care immediately and entered into a longitudinal ART register upon starting ART. The pre-ART register is no longer necessary. The ART register now includes additional data elements such as baseline CD4 count, TB preventive therapy start date, and active TB disease date. Hepatitis screening columns and third-line regimen switches have also been added. Viral load testing is recommended at 6 months, 12 months, and annually thereafter. Cross-sectional and cohort reports aggregate data from the ART register. Cross-sectional reports provide a snapshot of patient data at a specific time, while cohort reports track outcomes for groups of patients who started ART during the same period. These reports are essential for monitoring patient and program outcomes, identifying trends, and addressing gaps in care.
